h: Shale Bings and Country Parks of West Lothian
p: Those pinky-red hills you'll spot on the drive in are no accident. The Five Sisters are bings, huge heaps of spent shale left over from West Lothian's shale oil industry, which boomed in the nineteenth century after the chemist James Young worked out how to extract paraffin oil from the local rock. Today the bings are protected landmarks and havens for wildlife, and they give the zoo its name and a real sense of place.

If that history grabs you, the Almond Valley Heritage Centre in Livingston is home to the Museum of the Scottish Shale Oil Industry, alongside a farm with animals and play areas, so it's a natural second stop for families. Almondell and Calderwood Country Park, just east of the zoo near Mid Calder, follows the River Almond through wooded valleys and has easy riverside walks.

Further afield, Polkemmet Country Park near Whitburn has woodland trails and play space, and Beecraigs Country Park in the hills above Linlithgow has a deer farm, lochs and adventure trails. Linlithgow Palace, birthplace of Mary, Queen of Scots, is a superb ruin beside a loch and well worth the trip.

Getting there: West Calder has a railway station on the Edinburgh to Glasgow via Shotts line, but the zoo itself is easiest by car. Bring warm layers in any season, as the zoo stands on fairly high, open ground where the wind can bite.
